description: CouleeS Lab (Coulee Sky Lab) is physics student(s) exploring ways to make science accessible and learning how research can be conducted.
summary: CouleeS Lab (Coulee Sky Lab) is a free, public web tool that lets anyone explore NASA’s SPHEREx infrared sky and see how it changes over time. Users pan a live SPHEREx all-sky map or jump to coordinates, then open any 30′ grid square. CouleeS Lab asks NASA’s IRSA archive for every SPHEREx photo of that patch, aligns them on one grid, and lets you flip through them with a time bar. You can play them like a flipbook, blink two dates, stack each visit and subtract them, or spin a 3D “time cube” where moving objects trace slanted lines. Anyone can circle something that moves, link sightings of the same object across dates into a tracked path, and verify or vote down other people’s finds. Known brown dwarfs, Backyard Worlds discoveries, CatWISE movers, asteroids and planets are overlaid so nobody re-finds the known. It turns SPHEREx’s repeated all-sky scans into a citizen-science search for nearby brown dwarfs, fast stars and perhaps a distant Planet X.
details:
1. Sky map: NASA/IRSA’s SPHEREx all-sky map (102 infrared wavelengths, 0.75–5 µm, with a wavelength slider and presets), plus AllWISE, 2MASS and DSS for comparison. There’s an optional sky guide (constellations, Milky Way, Messier objects, bright named stars, tonight’s planets) so amateur astronomers can get their bearings.
  2. Fixed 30′ grid: everyone who opens the same square sees the same photos, annotations and comment thread. The selection box snaps to squares (or moves freely) and turns to match the sky’s curvature.
  3. Time-lapse viewer: the Python backend queries IRSA’s SIA service for every SPHEREx exposure covering the patch. It reads only the needed pixels from NASA’s cloud copy on AWS S3 (HTTP range requests), reprojects every frame onto a common grid with astropy/reproject, and serves them in time order. Tools include a time bar, play at any frame rate, blink, a colour-band (D1–D6) filter, median-stacking each visit with blink/difference views, and a rotatable three.js 3D time cube.
  4. Community science: draw a circle or square, then adjust and double-click to save. Each annotation gets a unique ULID plus an IAU-style designation. Sightings of one object on different dates link into a single object with a numbered path through time. Others can verify (3 checks → green) or vote “I don’t see it” (3 → removed, undoable). Creators can delete unverified marks. The annotation list is grouped by object, with filters.
  5. Don’t rediscover the known: SIMBAD brown dwarfs and high-proper-motion stars, Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 discoveries, NASA CatWISE fast movers, and JPL’s list of known asteroids in each photo. Planet positions are computed for each photo’s exact date. All are drawn where the object should be on that photo’s date (proper motion applied).
  6. Always current: frame lists refresh from NASA every few hours, so new SPHEREx releases appear automatically. A built-in demo pack keeps the judge demos working even when NASA’s servers are slow.
